blocks.recap_md: To apply a compound procedure to arguments, evaluate the body of the procedure with each formal parameter replaced by the corresponding argument - the substitution rule.
Worked example: substituting 5 for `a` in `f`'s body reduces `(f 5)` down to `(sum-of-squares 6 10)`.
Continuing the reduction through `square`'s definition and arithmetic, `(sum-of-squares 6 10)` reduces step by step to 136.
This process is the substitution model - a way to think about procedure application, not a description of how a real interpreter works, and it will eventually be replaced by more refined models.
An alternative model - fully expand operand expressions first, then reduce - reaches the same answer for `(f 5)` but re-evaluates some subexpressions more than once.
The 'expand then reduce' method is normal-order evaluation; Lisp actually uses applicative-order evaluation (evaluate arguments, then apply) for efficiency and simplicity.

knowledge_items.statement: To apply a compound procedure, evaluate its body with each formal parameter replaced by the corresponding argument - this is the substitution model for procedure application.

The substitution model is a way to think about what procedure application means, not a description of how a real interpreter works internally (which actually uses a local environment, not literal text substitution) - and it eventually breaks down once mutable data is introduced later in the book.

Normal-order evaluation ('fully expand, then reduce') and applicative-order evaluation ('evaluate arguments, then apply') give the same answer for substitution-model-compatible procedures, but normal-order can re-evaluate the same subexpression multiple times; Lisp uses applicative-order for efficiency and simplicity.

questions.prompt: To apply the compound procedure `f` (whose body is `(sum-of-squares (+ a 1) (* a 2))`) to the argument 5 under the substitution model, what's the first step?
options: Replace the formal parameter `a` with the argument 5 throughout the body, getting `(sum-of-squares (+ 5 1) (* 5 2))`
Immediately look up a cached result for `f` applied to 5, if one exists
Replace the procedure name `f` itself with the number 5
Evaluate `sum-of-squares` and `square` first as standalone expressions, ignoring the argument
questions.explanation: The substitution model applies a compound procedure by evaluating its body with each formal parameter replaced by the corresponding argument - here, replacing `a` with 5 throughout `f`'s body.

questions.prompt: According to the text, is the substitution model an accurate description of how a real Lisp interpreter evaluates procedure applications internally?
options: No - it's a way to help us think about what procedure application means; real interpreters use a local environment for the formal parameters instead of manipulating program text
Yes - every real Lisp interpreter literally rewrites the procedure's source text, substituting in the argument values
Yes, but only for procedures with exactly one formal parameter
No - real interpreters ignore formal parameters entirely and only look at argument order
questions.explanation: The text explicitly stresses that the purpose of substitution is to help us think about procedure application, not to describe how the interpreter really works - actual implementations use a local environment, as later chapters explain.

questions.prompt: Under normal-order evaluation (fully expand, then reduce) applied to `(f 5)`, what actually happens to subexpressions like `(+ 5 1)` compared to applicative-order evaluation?
options: They can get evaluated more than once, since substitution happens before any reduction, duplicating any operand expression that's used more than once in the body
They are evaluated exactly once, just like in applicative-order evaluation, with no difference in efficiency
They are never evaluated at all under normal-order evaluation
They are evaluated before the procedure name itself is looked up
questions.explanation: The text shows `(+ 5 1)` and `(* 5 2)` each get evaluated twice under normal-order evaluation, because `square`'s body `(* x x)` uses its parameter twice, duplicating whatever expression was substituted in - this repeated work is part of why Lisp uses applicative-order evaluation instead.
